case_name: CASE OF ANTI-CORRUPTION FOUNDATION (FBK) AND OTHERS v. RUSSIA

assessment.Interference with protected expression: This is a case of multiple direct interferences with Article 10 rights, not a positive-obligation case. The applicants formed the core of Mr Navalnyy’s anti-corruption and opposition network, which published online investigations, documentaries and political messaging, and promoted tactical voting and protest activity (see paragraphs 5-10). The freezing of accounts, seizure of equipment, “foreign agent” designation, administrative fine, and later “extremist” ban all had the practical effect of restricting the production and dissemination of political and anti-corruption speech (see paragraphs 19, 24, 29-32, 33-39).

assessment.Nature of the speech and level of protec: The expression at issue lay at the heart of Article 10 protection: allegations of corruption by high-ranking officials, criticism of those in power, election-related advocacy and online political campaigning (see paragraphs 6-7, 15, 35). Because the speech concerned matters of obvious public interest and the applicants acted as political activists and public watchdogs, the State’s margin of appreciation was narrow and especially weighty reasons were required to justify restrictions.

assessment.Freezing of bank accounts and searches: The money-laundering investigation was opened on vague allegations concerning unidentified persons and ATM deposits, without concrete facts showing that the individual applicants had engaged in criminal conduct (see paragraphs 12-16). Yet the courts froze all funds in the applicants’ accounts, and even newly opened accounts, so that the FBK could not pay salaries or continue its normal activities (see paragraphs 18-23). The search campaign was similarly sweeping: about 191 searches were conducted, including at homes of relatives, supporters and even an independent journalist, and devices and production equipment were seized (see paragraphs 24-28). Domestic law required courts to set out specific factual circumstances and, for urgent searches, to verify genuine urgency (see paragraphs 41, 44-46), but the courts used standard formulae, gave no individualised assessment, and accepted unsubstantiated claims of urgency (see paragraphs 20-28). That points to arbitrariness and serious doubt that these measures were truly “prescribed by law”; in any event, measures that disabled the applicants’ ability to function and publish were plainly disproportionate.

assessment.Foreign-agent designation and fine: The FBK was designated a “foreign agent” because of a relatively small transfer from an individual in Spain that reached its account after the earlier freezing measures and was later returned (see paragraphs 29-31). The organisation was then fined for non-compliance (see paragraph 32). For an NGO centrally engaged in anti-corruption investigations and political criticism, such a label was inherently stigmatising and likely to deter donors, staff and audiences. The domestic courts relied formalistically on the existence of the transfer and did not weigh the chilling effect on the organisation’s public-interest speech. That approach is difficult to reconcile with the Court’s assessment of the Russian “foreign agent” regime in comparable cases (see no. 39446/16).

assessment.Extremism designation and dissolution: The most serious interference was the use of extremism proceedings to suspend, dissolve and ban the applicants’ organisations (see paragraphs 33-36). The Moscow City Court relied on online dissemination, participation in unauthorised protests, calls to attend rallies supporting Mr Navalnyy, and involvement of minors, then characterised the organisations as extremist and aimed at violent overthrow of the constitutional order; the hearing was held in camera because classified material was used (see paragraph 35). On that basis, the FBK and FZPG were liquidated and the Navalnyy Headquarters network was prohibited, after interim suspension and placement on the extremism list even before the final ruling (see paragraph 34). Under the Court’s case-law, dissolution of an organisation for “extremism” requires convincing evidence of advocacy or use of violence, and overbroad reliance on vague extremism concepts is incompatible with pluralism (see no. 32401/10). Here, the reasons described in the facts largely concern opposition activity and protest mobilisation, not demonstrated incitement to violence sufficient to justify silencing a nationwide political movement.

assessment.Necessity and proportionality: Even assuming that the authorities pursued legitimate aims such as prevention of disorder or crime, national security, or protection of the rights of others, the domestic courts did not provide relevant and sufficient reasons. They failed to show an evidential link between most applicants and the alleged offences, targeted relatives and unrelated journalists, relied on secret or unspecified material, and imposed the most severe possible consequences on an opposition network operating in a context of protests and elections (see paragraphs 15, 18, 24-28, 33-39). The cumulative impact was extreme: total financial paralysis, seizure of means of communication, stigmatising labelling, dissolution, and subsequent criminal exposure for supporters and donors (see paragraphs 19, 24, 32, 35, 38-39). Less restrictive responses were not considered. The overall picture is therefore one of suppression of dissent rather than a pressing social need in a democratic society.

assessment.Conclusion: Taken together, the bank-account freezes and searches, the “foreign agent” designation and sanction, and especially the extremism ruling and its aftermath amounted to unjustified and disproportionate restrictions on political and anti-corruption expression. The domestic authorities did not apply Convention-compliant scrutiny and the measures had an obvious chilling effect on the applicants’ freedom of expression (see paragraphs 19, 24, 29-39; see also nos. 39446/16 and 32401/10).
